IOM welcomes this ministerial dialogue on drought and resilience and the recognition of the impacts of drought on human mobility.

Across the world, environmental pressures, including frequent and severe droughts, are eroding livelihoods and increasing pressure on people and ecosystems.

As conditions deteriorate, the number of people who face difficult choices about whether to move or stay is growing.

For some people, migration can provide new opportunities and become part of an adaptation strategy. For others, the priority is to have the conditions, services, and livelihoods that allow them to remain safely and sustainably in their communities. To better address these linkages, IOM is supporting Member States to integrate human mobility considerations into national drought frameworks and related planning instruments. But beyond this, we are supporting governments in translating policy commitments into innovative solutions, investment-ready programs, and partnerships that reduce displacement risk, strengthen resilience, and unlock sustainable development. IOM stands ready to continue working with member states, partner organizations, and affected communities to scale solutions, mobilize investment, and strengthen resilience and adaptation to drought where it matters most.

Mr. President, Excellencies, distinguished delegates, drought is among the most pervasive challenges of this century. It threatens food and water security, ecosystems, and livelihoods. Farmers, pastoralists, and dryland communities bear the heaviest cost. Climate change and pressure on land and water are making droughts more frequent, longer, and more severe. The response has too often been reactive. Countries act only once drought has hit, when the losses are already mounting. The shift the world needs is from response to preparedness. This begins with a fundamental change in approach. Drought cannot continue to be treated as a temporary emergency, managed after crops fail, livestock are lost, and water sources disappear. It must be addressed as a long-term risk within agricultural, water, land use, and development planning. Science already offers many of the tools required: early warning systems that anticipate risk, climate-informed water management, drought-resilient crops and farming systems, restored soils, rangelands and watersheds, and better evidence to direct investment where it can have the best and greatest impact. The challenge is to connect these solutions and deliver them at scale. That shift depends on evidence, and it depends on turning commitments into action. As governments work to agree to a global drought framework at COP17, CGIAR provides the science that can inform stronger negotiation positions and practical follow-through. At COP17, CGIAR is sharing evidence from Central, South and Southeast Asia, from Latin America, from the Middle East and North Africa, and from Sub-Saharan Africa on how drought risk information can trigger earlier coordinated action and how the integrated management of water, land and food systems can strengthen resilience. This matters because drought crosses sectors, landscapes, and borders. Our response must do the same, regional cooperation supported by strong institutions. The CGR supplies the science behind all of these systems. As parties shape the global response to drought, the CGIAR calls for three priorities, invest before crises occur, place science and early warning at the center of decision making and ensure preparedness reaches the farmers, pastoralists and communities facing the greatest risk. Thank you very much.

Representatives of international organizations, financial institutions and development partners, distinguished delegates, excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, on behalf of the Mongolian government, I extend my sincere appreciation to all participants in the ministerial dialogue on drought resilience convened as part of the Water Day at UNCCCT COP17. Thank you for your active engagement and valuable contributions. Drought is becoming more frequent, prolonged and severe, with cascading impacts on the water and food security, ecosystems, livelihoods, economies and human well-being. No country is immune. Drought is no longer an isolated environmental concern. It is global and systemic challenge. As land degradation intensifies, drought risk increases. As climate change accelerates, water scarcity deepens. As biodiversity is lost, ecosystem resilience declines. Drought therefore lies at the intersection of land, water, food, climate and development. Today's dialogue has reaffirmed one central message. We must shift from reacting to drought after it occurs to anticipating, preparing for and reducing risk before they become crises. For many countries, including Mongolia, Drought is already a present reality. Land degradation affects 81.9% of our territory and more than 428,000 people are exposed to drought impacts. For our 195,000 livestock herding households, healthy land, reliable water sources and drought preparedness are essential to their livelihoods and food security. We must remember that drought doesn't begin on the day the rain stops, nor is resilience built on the day an emergency is declared. Resilience must be established in advance through risk assessment, early warning, long-term policies and sustained investment. Today's discussion highlighted five priorities. First, we need integrated approaches. Sustainable land and water management, ecosystem restoration and resilient agriculture must be embedded in national development. climate adaptation and land restoration planning. Second, science, data and early warning must be led anticipatory action. Stronger monitoring, forecasting and reliable data supported by innovation and artificial intelligence can enable timely evidence-based decisions. Third, international and regional cooperation is indispensable. We must strengthen coordination, knowledge sharing, technical assistance and capacity building, particularly for drought vulnerable countries and communities. Fourth, financing must match the scale of the challenge. We need significantly greater and more predictable financing for drought. resilience through innovative financing mechanisms, stronger partnerships with international financial institutions and better alignment of climate development and drought related investments. Fifth, drought resilience requires whole of the government and whole of the society approach. Women, Youth, farmers, pastoralists, and other vulnerable groups must participate meaningfully in planning and decision making. Particular attention must also be given to groundwater. In many regions, it is the last reliable source of the water for communities, food production, livestock, and ecosystems. Its importance doesn't justify our exploration. It demands responsible management. We must ensure that extraction remains within sustainable recharge, limits and protect the connection between groundwater, surface water and ecosystems. Existing initiatives, including the International Drought Resilience Alliance, The International Drought Resilience Observatory and Drought Financing Mechanisms provide a strong foundation. Our priority now is to translate these initiatives, resources and partnerships into concrete action at the local, national and regional levels. Mongolians have long revered water as Chandman Erden, appreciates Wishful filling jewel. Our ancestors taught us when rivers run dry, the land withers. When the land withers, life itself fades. Our message is simple. Without water, we cannot restore degraded land. Without healthy land, we cannot ensure water security. Without protecting both together, We cannot build resilience to drought. It is in this spirit that Mongolia launched the Water and Land Nexus Initiative. Today at UNCCCT COP17, bringing together science, policy, investment, and practical solutions for collective action. Drought may be the natural phenomenon, But if there it becomes the disaster depends on the choices we make today. May this dialogue strengthen our shared resolve and help COP17 advance a forward-looking decision that turns commitments into action. Let us restore land and restore hope. Thank you.
